title: Meta’s new commercial terms say if its AI makes a mistake, it will legally be the customer’s fault
summary: In Meta commercial terms changes slated to kick in on October 30, the company will shift the liability for any mistakes made by its AI models to its enterprise customers. The new language also makes those IT executives responsible for anything done by a partner or contractor. The changes also finally put a stake into the heart of robots.txt, with Meta granting itself the right to grab, and use for its own purposes, any content associated with a Meta account. The language allows Meta to “use automated software such as web scrapers, bots, robots, spiders, crawlers, and user agents and create test credentials to access, index, cache, analyze, collect, retrieve, or crawl the domains, web pages, or URLs, and any content available through them, that are associated with your products or services,” according to the new language on its website on Monday . Meta also wants to be able to “periodically pull updates from such domains, web pages, or URLs in order to provide, develop, improve, research, and maintain advertising and business products including business, commercial and related products to help you create and deliver ads and other commercial content.” Consultants said the three biggest concerns they had about the changes were the web scraping, data ownership, and AI liability transfer. Web scraping and data ownership However, Meta emailed a statement to CIO.com late Monday suggesting that it was rethinking its position on web scraping. Saying that Meta wanted “to clarify” the web scraping changes, Emil Vazques, a Meta public affairs manager, said, “ the crawling terms we consolidated only applied to our ads and business products and we’ve clarified that in the terms themselves. It does not change how Meta uses web crawlers. As always, content owners can use robots.txt to signal their preferences . title: Don’t be fooled. The AI that was supposed to save us time is doing just the opposite | Gaby Hinsliff
summary: The government says it can transform the state with AI, but it is no match for the resulting stream of machine-generated slop. And we all pay the cost Another morning, another avalanche of emails. Even after a guilty cull, my inbox is sitting at well over 7,000, but lately I’ve started subscribing to the Quentin Crisp theory of housework: why bother, when after four years or so you stop noticing the accumulating dust? Empty inboxes just fill up again anyway. In theory, email was supposed to save hours of meetings, phone calls and standing over photocopiers. Instead, we just spend hours deleting stuff people wouldn’t have bothered telling us if it had meant picking up the phone, but which they can now spam to their entire database at the click of a button. The glorious ease and convenience of being able to reach the world in seconds came, we now know, with the inconvenience of them being able to reach you right back. title: AI didn’t create your IT data problem, it just exposed it
summary: When an AI pilot in IT operations underdelivers, the first instinct is to question the technology. Was the model wrong? Did the tool overpromise? Did the team pick the wrong use case? Those are fair questions. But in many organizations, the answer sits somewhere less glamorous: in a configuration management database that hasn’t been reconciled in two years, in asset data in spreadsheets, or in a service desk where three teams use the same category field in three different ways. Transform fragmented IT data into the trusted data foundation AI needs → AI doesn’t create these problems. It surfaces them quickly and publicly. The silo problem nobody owns Most IT environments grew one tool at a time. The endpoint team adopted a management platform. Security brought in a scanner. Service management built workflows in the ITSM tool. Procurement tracked purchases in its own system. Each decision made sense on its own. Few were ever designed to share data with one another. The result is a landscape where every team holds a partial view of the same environment . The endpoint console shows 9,400 devices. The scanner sees 8,700. The CMDB lists 10,200, including hundreds retired long ago. Nobody is exactly wrong, but nobody is complete. People have learned to work around these gaps. An experienced analyst knows which system to trust for which question and fills in the rest from memory. That institutional knowledge is valuable, but it’s invisible to AI. And that’s where the trouble starts. The gaps are organizational, too Fragmentation isn’t only technical. Ivanti’s 2026 State of Cybersecurity research found that 48% of security professionals say IT teams don’t respond urgently to security concerns, and 40% say IT lacks an understanding of the organization’s risk tolerance. Those aren’t tooling gaps. They’re alignment gaps, and they shape how data is collected, labeled, and maintained across every system AI will eventually draw from. title: The Googlebook work test: Can an Android laptop get the job done?
summary: In a weird way, I’ve been thinking about the idea of a Googlebook for well over a decade now — despite the fact that such a product has only officially existed for a matter of months. I’m relatively unusual in the world of tech journalism, y’see, in that I’ve been both writing about Android and ChromeOS since the platforms’ earliest days and actively using devices from both ends of those ecosystems in my own day-to-day life that entire time. Most tech writers tend to be iPhone owners and Chromebook skeptics who see this part of the digital world from an outside view — once a year or so, when significant new devices come along for assessment — without having the perspective of someone who’s truly immersed in it day in and day out. That distinction is always painfully apparent when you read a review that waxes on endlessly with out-of-touch iPhone comparisons and comments about the limiting nature of Google’s ChromeOS concept — positions that simply aren’t accurate for those of us who live in these ecosystems and embrace the philosophies they offer. This won’t be one of those reviews, and I perhaps more than anyone have been champing at the bit to get my hands on one of Google’s new Android-ChromeOS-combining Googlebooks since the vaguest concept of these devices first appeared on the horizon earlier this year. So keep that in mind when I tell you, coming from the perspective of someone who very much wanted to love this: Using a Googlebook is an extraordinarily strange experience — especially when you’re treating it like a regular laptop, as it’s being positioned by Google, and relying on it to get real work done. But amidst all the oddness, there are some true high points along with plenty of intriguing, if unfinished-feeling, potential. title: Follow the money: Who benefits from the UK’s Apple Pay crackdown?
summary: The UK wants to take a chunk out of Apple Pay, as the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) moves to force Apple to open access to its 12-year-old contactless payment system to rivals. The regulator has published a consultation document that proposes requiring Apple to allow competitors to use the near-field communication (NFC) chip on its devices to enable alternative payment systems on iOS on “fair, reasonable, transparent and non-discriminatory terms.” The regulator says action is required because UK businesses have complained that Apple’s existing NFC access arrangements are not commercially viable. 30% of UK adults use Apple Pay ? The regulator also revealed some interesting statistics concerning use of contactless tech in the UK: Contactless payments represent 39% of all payments , compared to just 3% of transactions a decade ago. 62% of adults currently use a digital wallet. 50% of those use Apple Wallet — which implies that around 30% of UK adults use Apple Pay. “These proposals open the door to more innovation, more choice and economic growth, including in the UK’s important fintech sector,” said Sarah Cardell, chief executive of the CMA. It’s not clear if those companies will take advantage of this forced liberalization. The CMA tells us that the only services that have done so in the EU, where Apple has already been forced to open up NFC, have all been transnational entities, including Vipps, PayPal, Klarna, Curve, and BBVA. Are consumers flocking to these services to rejoice in this new market liberalization? While this open NFC has only been in place a few months, I don’t think so. Who will really benefit from this? title: Enterprise AI needs more than an AI engineer
summary: Anthropic has a $100 million plan to help enterprises get more from AI. No, it doesn’t involve agents. It involves people. Lots of people. How retro. On October 2, the company announced Claude Frontier Academy , with a goal of training 10,000 frontier deployed engineers by the end of 2027. Participants work through a simulated deployment, including use-case selection, security review, and handover, before undertaking a 12-week residency on a real project at their own company. For a business selling increasingly capable models, it’s telling that Anthropic recognizes some of the thorniest problems in AI don’t involve AI at all. This, to me, is indicative of real progress, because the heart of any technological shift is always people. Which people? Well, that’s where this idea becomes particularly interesting. As critical as developers are to the success of AI in any particular organization, we need those developers working alongside the people who understand the business, with authority to turn that understanding into systems that other employees can use. That’s the key to AI success. Old advice for a new assignment It has always been thus, however much we try to pretend that this time it’s different. Back in 2013, I quoted Gartner analyst Svetlana Sicular discoursing on the rise of big data technologies like Hadoop: “Organizations already have people who know their own data better than mystical data scientists.” She continued, “Learning Hadoop is easier than learning the company’s business.” Data becomes useful when paired with industry expertise—from experts who understand which data actually matters. This topic is perpetually relevant. I covered the argument in 2023 and again in 2025 . We’ve always needed people who can translate business requirements into software. AI expands the kinds of knowledge that software can work with. Language models extend that work to material that often sat outside our applications: research notes, meeting transcripts, internal debates

title: The local computing rebellion
summary: Take a close look at your monthly software bills. The charges that once seemed small and separate can add up to a new kind of dependency: subscriptions for word processing, creative tools, storage, and now AI features bundled into products, whether you asked for them or not. For many people, it’s no longer a choice between buying software or renting it. The software they used to run on a PC increasingly depends on an account, an internet connection, a cloud service, or a particular plan. Even when an application runs locally, its essential features may rely on online authentication, remote storage, or services that can change without much notice. Microsoft and Adobe are prominent examples of this shift. Their subscriptions offer real benefits, including frequent updates, collaboration, and access across devices. But people who are looking for a dependable word processor or video editor can find themselves navigating bundles, account requirements, cloud storage prompts, and AI features they don’t want. Users are growing frustrated that they have little choice about being forced into cloud services. Interest in local computing The response is a renewed interest in local computing: software that runs on a person’s own computer, stores work where they choose, and does not require a recurring payment for basic use. This isn’t a rejection of cloud computing. It’s a demand for a more balanced relationship between local machines and remote services. Home users and small businesses are turning to open source and other locally installed applications. They may not offer every advanced feature of a commercial suite, but many users don’t need every feature. If a free, locally run tool can handle the work, then “good enough” can be a rational decision. The same logic applies to AI . Some users want powerful models hosted in the cloud. title: When ‘access denied’ becomes an agent’s next objective
summary: One line from a recent AI incident caught my attention. Describing how an OpenAI agent got into a Medicare statistics portal, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said it “ didn’t accept no for an answer .” It sounds almost funny. In software terms, though, it points to a real problem. An access control said no, and the agent treated the answer as information about how to continue. “The AI agent found a way around those blocks,” Albanese said. The agent accessed public and non-public files, according to the prime minister , though Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles said the information was “not particularly sensitive.” An investigation is underway. Around the same time, OpenAI disclosed another incident . A model in training found its web searches and direct connections blocked, then discovered that the environment’s own DNS resolver still answered. It embedded questions in hostnames and got answers from an external chatbot. OpenAI stopped the run . Days later, it shelved GPT-6.1 Astra , which Saachi Jain , its head of safety systems, said “didn’t quite meet the bar in terms of staying within scope and authorization.” Different systems, different failures, one question: what does “access denied” mean to an agent? Why a denial is information Traditional software treats an authorization failure as the end of a code path. A service gets a 403, raises an exception and someone reads the log. The denial works as a stop sign because the program has no independent objective to pursue. Agents do have one. We have spent years teaching software to recover from failure: retry the request, switch the endpoint, back off and try again. Those are good instincts. They become dangerous when the failure is the security control itself.
